topics: 👗 The Priest's Daughter Who Married Out — her liability for eating teruma, and how her death penalty can still change
🚫 Two Exceptions to the Provisional Guilt Offering — defiling the Temple, and the reach of Yom Kippur's atonement
🕊️ Does Yom Kippur Atone Without Repentance? — a dispute reconciled through Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's own two positions
🗣️ Does the Blasphemer Bring an Offering? — Rabbi Akiva reads karet 'in the place of an offering'; the Rabbis disagree
🤰 Which Miscarriages Require a Sin Offering? — the new mishna sorts fetal forms into eaten, not eaten, and exempt

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Boundaries of Liability, Atonement, and a New Mishna on Miscarriage
overview.subtitle: Keritot 7a–7b
overview.hebrewSource: יֵשׁ מְבִיאוֹת קׇרְבָּן וְנֶאֱכָל, וְיֵשׁ מְבִיאוֹת קׇרְבָּן וְאֵינוֹ נֶאֱכָל, וְיֵשׁ שֶׁאֵינָם מְבִיאוֹת
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by finishing the anointing-oil discussion with the case of a priest's daughter who eats teruma after marrying out of the priesthood, then returns to the original mishna's list of exceptions: why the one who defiles the Temple does not bring a provisional guilt offering for uncertainty, and whether the same exclusion should apply to a sin whose Yom Kippur has already passed. This opens into a broader debate about whether Yom Kippur atones even without repentance, and a related dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis over whether the unwitting blasphemer must bring a sin offering at all. The daf then turns a corner entirely: a new mishna opens tractate Keritot's discussion of the sin offering a woman brings after childbirit or miscarriage, classifying which fetal forms obligate an offering that may be eaten, which obligate one that may not, and which exempt her entirely.

slides.title: 👗 The Priest's Daughter Who Married Out
slides.subtitle: Her liability shifts with her marital status — a case tied to the earlier dispute over anointing 'strangers'
rows: Married an Israelite (still eligible to return to teruma if widowed/divorced childless)
Burning — she retains her priestly status conceptually

callout.label: Connected dispute:
callout.text: Rav Yosef links this to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's disagreement over anointing a 'stranger': Rabbi Yehuda requires the person to be a stranger from beginning to end, which is why the Rabbis (aligned with his view) still treat her, in some sense, as a priest's daughter.

slides.title: 🚫 Two Exceptions to the Provisional Guilt Offering
slides.subtitle: The mishna excludes one case explicitly — should Yom Kippur create another?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna's stated exception: one who defiles the Temple or its sacred food does not bring a provisional guilt offering — he already owes a sliding-scale offering for the definite case
2️⃣ Proposed addition: shouldn't the mishna also exclude one whose Yom Kippur has passed, since Yom Kippur already atoned for any possible sin?

3️⃣ Reish Lakish: correct — but the mishna's exceptions cover cases where a sin still exists and the Torah exempts it anyway; after Yom Kippur, the sin no longer exists at all, so it needs no separate mention
4️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees: the true case needing exclusion is one who rejects Yom Kippur's atonement outright — for him, atonement does not take effect, so he would still owe an offering later

callout.label: Underlying question:
callout.text: Can Yom Kippur atone for a sin the sinner insists it should not atone for? This launches the next major debate.

slides.title: 🕊️ Does Yom Kippur Atone Without Repentance?
slides.subtitle: Two baraitot in the Sifra appear to contradict each other

lines.speaker: Baraita 1
lines.text: By logical inference from sin and guilt offerings (which atone only for those who repent), Yom Kippur too should atone only for the penitent.

lines.speaker: Baraita 2
lines.text: 'It is Yom Kippur' (Lev. 23:27) — atones in any case, regardless of fasting, labor, or repentance.

lines.speaker: Abaye's resolution
lines.text: No contradiction: the first baraita reflects Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's report of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion; the second reflects Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's own view — that Yom Kippur atones even without repentance, except for three severe sins (denying God, twisting Torah meaning, breaking the covenant of circumcision).

lines.speaker: Rava's resolution
lines.text: Both baraitot state Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's own view; he concedes only that Yom Kippur cannot atone for the very transgression of desecrating Yom Kippur itself — since a person eating or working on Yom Kippur may die before daytime atonement can apply.

callout.label: Related retraction:
callout.text: Rava initially held that a sin offering atones even if its owner insists 'let it not atone for me' — but retracted this after finding a baraita showing such a stipulation blocks atonement.

slides.title: 🗣️ Does the Blasphemer Bring an Offering?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis dispute whether an unwitting blasphemer needs a sin offering

boxes.title: Rabbi Akiva — liable
items: Karet for blasphemy (Numbers 15:30) is written in a passage that discusses an offering — that placement itself teaches liability
The Rabbis' challenge (why then not Pesach/milah, which also carry karet?) is answered: it's specifically karet near an offering-context that counts

boxes.title: The Rabbis — exempt
items: Blasphemy involves no physical action — 'one law for him who acts unwittingly' (Numbers 15:29) excludes pure speech
The karet clause instead teaches, by verbal analogy ('shall bear his sin'), that one who misses the second Paschal offering is liable to karet

callout.label: A second dispute:
callout.text: Isi ben Yehuda reads 'blasphemes the Lord' as comparing the sinner to one who damages God's own 'bowl' (a severe image); Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya reads it more mildly, and elsewhere even identifies the verse's blasphemer with an idol worshipper — against the Rabbis, who insist it means one who curses God's Name.

slides.title: 🤰 Which Miscarriages Require a Sin Offering?
slides.subtitle: The new mishna opens with three categories, based on the form of what was miscarried
rows: Fetus shaped like a domesticated/undomesticated animal or bird (R' Meir) — the Rabbis require human form; a 'sandal' fetus, placenta, developed amniotic sac, or fetus emerging in pieces; also a Canaanite maidservant, derived from the extra word 'woman'
Miscarrying an unidentified mass; or two women miscarrying together where only one type obligates an offering and it's unknown which — unless (R' Yosei) both stood together, in which case it is eaten

Amniotic sac full of water, blood, or discolored matter; fetus shaped like fish, locusts, or vermin; miscarriage on day forty; a caesarean birth (though R' Shimon obligates this last case, deriving it from a seemingly superfluous 'she bears')

callout.label: Practical footnote:
callout.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel go on to dispute a related case: one who miscarries on the night before her eighty-first day (when offerings normally cannot be brought) — Beit Hillel obligate her in a second offering, Beit Shammai exempt her, arguing the night was never fit for sacrifice at all.

summary.principle: The Gemara closes its analysis of exceptions to the provisional guilt offering and of Yom Kippur's atoning power, then opens a new mishna precisely classifying which forms of miscarriage obligate a woman's sin offering — and whether that offering may be eaten.

flowSteps.content: 👗 A priest's daughter who married out keeps a partial priestly status depending on the marriage's permanence
🚫 The mishna's sole stated exception (Temple defilement) prompts debate over whether Yom Kippur creates another
🕊️ Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: Yom Kippur atones even without repentance, except for three severe sins and for desecrating Yom Kippur itself

columns.content: 🗣️ Rabbi Akiva derives an offering for blasphemy from karet's placement near a sacrifice; the Rabbis exempt him for lacking an action
🤰 The new mishna sorts miscarried forms into eaten, not-eaten, and exempt categories

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: liability for an offering always tracks the precise wording and placement of its verse, never a general impression

quiz.q: According to the Rabbis (as opposed to Rabbi Meir), what happens to a priest's daughter who married a man permanently disqualifying her from returning to the priesthood, if she then unwittingly eats teruma?
o: She pays principal and an added fifth, and her death penalty is strangulation
She pays only the principal, with no added fifth, and her death penalty is burning
She is entirely exempt from any payment
She must divorce her husband immediately
quiz.e: The Rabbis hold that regardless of whom she married, she pays only the principal without the added fifth, and her death penalty remains burning, as she retains a conceptual tie to her priestly lineage.

quiz.q: According to Reish Lakish, why doesn't the mishna list 'one whose sin occurred before Yom Kippur' among its exceptions to the provisional guilt offering, the way it lists the Temple-defiler?
o: Because Yom Kippur never atones for unwitting sins
Because after Yom Kippur has passed, there is no longer any sin remaining to require exclusion — Yom Kippur already atoned for it
Because the Temple-defiler case is unrelated to sin offerings
Because provisional guilt offerings are brought only on Yom Kippur
quiz.e: Reish Lakish explains that the mishna's stated exceptions involve genuine unresolved sins that the Torah exempts from an offering; after Yom Kippur, the sin itself is already atoned for, so there is nothing left to exclude.

quiz.q: According to Rava's final resolution, for which transgression does even Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi agree that Yom Kippur cannot atone, regardless of repentance?
o: Idol worship
Forbidden relations
Transgressing the prohibitions of Yom Kippur itself (such as eating or working on it)
Theft
quiz.e: Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi must concede that Yom Kippur cannot atone for the desecration of Yom Kippur itself, since the sinner might die before the day's atoning power can take effect.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Akiva, why is an unwitting blasphemer liable to bring a sin offering despite committing no physical action?
o: Because blasphemy always involves striking someone
Because the karet stated for blasphemy (Numbers 15:30) is written in a passage that discusses bringing an offering
Because the Rabbis agree with him on this point
Because blasphemy is punished the same as idol worship
quiz.e: Rabbi Akiva reasons that since the Torah could have stated karet for blasphemy anywhere, its placement specifically within a passage about offerings teaches that an offering is required.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, which of the following miscarriages requires NO sin offering at all?
o: A fetus with the form of a domesticated animal
A 'sandal' fetus (flat, fish-like form)
An amniotic sac full of water
A fetus that emerged cut into pieces
quiz.e: The mishna lists an amniotic sac full of water (or blood, or discolored matter) among the cases requiring no sin offering at all, along with fetuses shaped like fish, locusts, or vermin, and a miscarriage on day forty.
